title: Vanishing of mutual information with an almost-surely constant variable
statement: Let $X \colon \Omega \to S$ and $Y \colon \Omega \to T$ be measurable random variables taking values in countable spaces, defined on a space $\Omega$ carrying a probability measure $\mu$ (or the zero measure), and suppose each of $X$ and $Y$ takes only finitely many values. If $Y$ is $\mu$-almost-surely equal to a fixed constant $c \in T$, then the mutual information between $X$ and $Y$ vanishes: \[ I[X : Y \,;\, \mu] = 0. \]
hypotheses_covered: X, Y measurable into countable measurable-singleton spaces
μ is zero or a probability measure
Y is μ-a.e. equal to a constant c
replaced: If $Y =^{\mu\text{-a.e.}} c$ for some constant $c : T$, then $I[X : Y;\mu] = 0$.
